messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Help with Fixed and Random Factors in procD.lm
messages.body_plain:
Your data might already show spatial dependence in a variogram and you can always plot variability among data points vs distance before generating any matrices.

In addition to the raw data variogram from above, it might also be helpful to use an AIC approach to choose among a set spatial dependence structures by creating variograms from the residuals of alternative models. This is important to take covariates into account. Included among these alternative models you can compare a model with no spatial dependence and this is preferable to only picking one matrix. For example, residuals from models with exponential decay of correlations among sites will have a different pattern than the same but with Gaussian decay of similarities among sites, but both might perform better or similar to a model without spatial dependence (this is data specific).

Cheers,
Bryan

messages.body_plain:
Dear Mike,

I ran the script with your new update for pairwise function and the test.type "stdist" worked fine. Although this statistics recovered lower p-values compared to test.type "dist", the paired comparisons were still non significant, although the PGLS ANOVA was significant. As you pointed out, I believe what explains these results are the low values of the effect size (Z) - Z scores were not greater than 1.8.
Thank you very much for your help and, considering my data, the standardized distances and the respectives p-values were congruent with the effect sizes, meaning that the comparison of slope vectors by standardized distances appears to be promising.
Sincerely,

Daniel

Em sex., 27 de set. de 2024 às 10:22, Michael Collyer <rrpp.c...@gmail.com> escreveu:

> Dear Daniel et al.,
>
> I have updated RRPP::summary.pairwise to include “stdist” as an option for comparison of slope vectors.  You can install RRPP from Github and the your analysis should work now.  I have not yet updated the Mahalanobis distance option (“mdist”) but that is up next.  Although I made this update, I do so with a little trepidation.
>
> The reason for my trepidation is that I am not comfortable with the multivariate generalization that is inherently assumed.  For example, with parametric multi-mean comparisons, there are different statistics that can be used but one is a pairwise t-statistic that looks a two-sample t-statistic for independent samples, substituting the MSE from a linear model for the pooled variance from two independent samples.  Either the “stdist” or “mdist” options are multivariate generalizations of this concept, using the trace or the determinant of the MSE matrix, respectively.
>
> There is similarly a two-sample t-statistic for comparing slopes from independent regressions.  This statistic looks just like the two-sample t-statistic for independent means, substituting slopes for means.  But I don’t really know of an analogous pairwise slopes test in an ANOVA or MANOVA framework using t-statistics substituting MSE for pooled variance of slopes.  I believe the reason for this is probably a practical matter.  If one were to attempt to perform an ANCOVA and learn there is heterogeneity among slopes, they would probably be compelled to perform different linear regressions by group, and subsequently compare slopes with two-sample t-tests for slopes.
>
> Therefore, I am making the assumption that (1) because a pairwise t-test for means substitutes MSE for pooled variance from independent samples, and (2) the pooled variance between independent samples for slopes has the same calculation as between means, then (3) it makes sense to calculate the pooled SE for a “stdist” test comparing slopes with the MSE matrix from a linear model that contains parameters for a group factor and covariate, plus interaction.  Furthermore, because coefficients for slopes and means are basically the same thing in a linear model — the numerator in the standardized distance is based on the cross-product of a vector that is the difference between vectors of coefficients — the “stdist” calculation applied to either slopes or means is mathematically commensurate.
>
> I cannot find a reason this logic is flawed but it could be because I am missing something obvious.  I am willing to take the chance because of the first principle soundness of calculation.  Hopefully I am not missing something!
>
> Hope this works for you!
> Mike

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am currently conducting a morphometric analysis of flowers from five palm species. My objective is to assess the taxonomic boundaries among these species and to analyze the intraspecific variation in their floral structures. Based on my observations, I have identified three levels of variation: species-level differences, individual-level differences, and the positional variation of flowers within the inflorescence (e.g., basal, medial, or apical positions).
I would appreciate any advice on how to quantify the variation explained by each of these levels. This is my first time working with geometric morphometrics, so I am open to any suggestions or recommendations you may have.

Thank you in advance for your help.

Gabriel

Hi everyone,
I analyzed shape variation in my data with morphol.disparity() function when suddenly something seemed wrong with the function. The function worked well while argument seed = n  was not provided. However, when I added the seed argument the function returned the following error.
Error: block factor not the same length as the number of observations.

Regards,
Mihajlo

gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(Y.gpa, species = plethodon$species,

Hi Federico,

Great, almost there. First, I provide a better alternative, then I respond to your questions.

Using cov_spatial:
cov.spatial is now defunct, but you can use something like
library(convoSPAT)
#https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/convoSPAT/versions/1.2.7/topics/cov_spatial
cov_matrix <- cov_spatial(dist_matrix, cov.model = "gaussian")

procD.lm(TGU.AFA$symm.shape ~ TGU1$LID + TGU1$sexo, Cov = cov_matrix, iter = 9999, RRPP = TRUE, SS.type = "III")

cov_spatial outputs a spatial covariance matrix and does not require supplied values of the variance or phi. Please be careful and note that cov_spatial requires the supplied dist_matrix to be scaled. Next, I would change the cov.model argument in cov_spatial() to other models and use AIC to see which spatial dependence structure gives the best model fit.

To respond to your concerns:
There is no requirement for SS or MS to be particular values in regression, the magnitude is completely dependent on the data and model. That said, if the high values of SS and MS surprise you, there may be an issue with the units or scaling at some point in your pipeline, I would double check you supplied the right inputs to each function. The values might have blown up because you used PC scores, which scale the data and this might result in unexpected changes, but that is only a wild guess.

I am not sure what you mean by "the coefficients suggest a total loss of the geometric shape of the analyzed structure". A final note about your pipeline is that it confounds spatial dependence with the covariates in your model (sex and LID). For this reason, people usually interpret variograms of the residuals for learning about model fits.

Shape data and variograms:
Using PC1 for the variogram is limiting, you should use all the data going into your final model instead. I am not sure if there is a function out there for easily and correctly obtaining a variogram from shape data, but you could always plot this manually. This would entail estimating the semivariance is 0.5*var(pairs), where pairs is the set of all pairwise distances among points a specific distance apart. This can be repeated n(n-1)/2 times across all pairs of n distinct locations, then you can plot semivariance vs distance. Each individual pairwise distance should be the procrustes distance, which is outputted by gpagen(). So, you are set for plotting the variogram for the raw data.

There might be an easy way of doing the same for model residuals, but I do not know exactly how off the top of my head. More knowledgeable folks on the list can give better advice than I and comment on whether estimating procrustes distances between individuals from the residuals makes sense to begin with.

Hope that helps!
Bryan

messages.subject: Evolutionary rates test
messages.body_plain:
Dear geomorph community,

I am trying to compare evolutionary rates among different groups (diet regimes) both for bodymass and shape (Procrustes coords). I am using the compare.evol.rates function and the output is:

Call: Observed Rate Ratio: 12.3879 P-value: 0.027 Effect Size: 2.0575 Based on 1000 random permutations The rate for group vert is 0.0391957025021914 The rate for group herb is 0.485551911564016
The rate for group omniv is 0.0691446613249569 The rate for group invert is 0.143925810067351

If I am not mistaken, the p-value and the Z effect are related to the ratio between max and min evolutionary rate. Is there any way to test if the rates observed for the groups are significally different from the mean evoluitionary rate?

Thank you very much.

Vasco Avramo

messages.subject: Measurement.error() and ICCstats() impementation
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I wish to implement new functionalities as described in
Collyer and Adams, 2024. The data I am working with was collected two years ago
so I would avoid digitizing it again due to probable bias. While this kind of “post-hoc”
analysis is not the intended use, we decided to use it as precedent for further
studies.

Data is organized in two segments of ontogeny, each
containing individuals on few consecutive developmental stages. The first
segment uses 7 landmarks with 14 semi-landmarks, no symmetry, the second
segment uses 11 landmarks with 16 semi-landmarks, bilateral symmetry. There are
two replicates, the second replicate covering 50% of total individuals. After
balancing out the sample, I am left with 9 individuals per stage in first and
12 individuals per stage in second segment.

I would like to obtain an estimate on Systematic ME and Systematic
ME:Groups and, if possible, the estimate of ICC values.

I am not sure if the number of replicates is adequate for
this methodology. As measurement.error() is able to handle high-dimensional
data, there should be no problem concerning number of individuals per group (developmental
stage).

Another uncertainty I have is should I perform repeatability
estimate on the whole segment as the developmental stages in question are
probably different in shape? If not, will estimate using ICCstats() on subsets of data for
each developmental stage be sound approach?

Any kind of insight is more than welcome.

Kind regards,

Marko

messages.body_plain:
Dear Marko,

There is no explicit need for balance in the measurement.error() function, and theoretically it should work even if certain subjects have no replication (only one observation).  Having said that, I’m not sure how trustworthy the results could be in many subjects only have one replicate and, therefore, contribute invariance to estimates of systematic ME.  If your question is whether it is okay that the number of replicates differ among subjects, my feeling is that it’s okay so long as the number of replicates is larger than 1 and I suspect that disparity among replicates per subject is mitigated if there are many replicates.  For example, having the number of replicates vary between 7-10 would be a better circumstance than between 2-4, in general.

Balance is more important for calculating ICC.  Additionally, and this might not be a shared opinion, I cannot perceive the circumstances where ICC is more appropriate than ANOVA with measurement.error(), and in most cases, I would warn that ICC is dangerous.  Here is why, via example.  Imagine ICC is measured with a few mouse skulls and 3-4 researchers digitizing skulls, and the value is a bit low for comfort.  To the sample of mouse skulls a dog skull is added, because the researchers are interested in the repeatability of the researchers to quantify mammal skull shape.  Suddenly the ICC is great, even though the mouses skull digitizations were not changed.  Is this reasonable?  Or does it falsely reassure the researchers that they are doing the same thing?  All they did was shrink the replicate variation relative to the subject variation.  Real digitization variation was not removed, it was masked by the variation among subjects used.

The ANOVA with measurement.error() HOLDS SUBJECT VARIATION CONSTANT and tests systematic ME independent of subject variation.  ICC stats can be misleading because they cannot account for subject variation in their calculation.

There might be cases where ICC is useful but I would not rely on it for inferences about measurement error.

Best,
Mike

If I do not do this,  I receive all TRUE if checking names using %in% but mostly FALSE if using == (e.g., rownames(Metadata) %in% Tree$tip.label returns TRUE but  rownames(Metadata) == Tree$tip.label doesn't).
I just wanted to make sure that all the data will be attributed to correct species when assessing the geomorph data frame if I don't match the order of the species names before import?
Sorry if I have missed this being asked before.
Thank you!

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] geomorph data frame creation
messages.body_plain:
Dear Phoebe,

The procD.pgls function requires matching of tree tip names and rownames/names of data and will sort a covariance matrix to match the order of observations based on the matched names.  Although I cannot guess why an error was alleviated by using a geomorph data frame, I can attest that using a geomorph data frame alleviates many possible errors.  Using a data frame precisely describes the environment in which the analysis is performed.  It means the function does not have to search for a variable or data in the global environment and try to make sense of it.

Best,
mike
